n: Holy Redeemer Church and Community Centre
w: Fernando Menis carved this raw concrete cluster from a neglected 1970s neighbourhood, fusing a church, community centre and square into rugged monolithic blocks pierced by coloured glass. Fifteen years in the making, it won the 2025 World Building of the Year for turning sacred architecture into a social anchor.
s: Rugged concrete church named world's best building
why: Named 2025 World Building of the Year by the World Architecture Festival

w: MAD Architects wrapped George Lucas's passion project in over 1,500 curved fiberglass panels, a smooth white form that appears to levitate over an 11-acre park. Structurally topped out in 2025, it houses illustration, comics, film and photography under a swooping roofline unlike anything else on the LA skyline.
s: A levitating white cloud of a museum
why: George Lucas's long-awaited narrative-art museum, structurally complete in 2025

w: At 377 metres and 82 storeys, this slender glass hotel opened in November 2025 as the world's tallest, its faceted form rising sheer above the Marina skyline. Guests reach one of the planet's highest infinity pools near the summit, looking straight down the canyon of towers that made Dubai Marina famous.
s: World's tallest hotel, 377m over the Marina
why: Opened November 2025 as the world's tallest hotel

w: Farshid Moussavi's first US Ismaili Centre unfolds as folded stone and glass volumes around gardens open to visitors of every faith. Dedicated in November 2025, it is the seventh Ismaili Centre worldwide and the first in the United States, conceived as much as civic meeting ground as prayer space.
s: First Ismaili Centre built in the United States
why: Dedicated November 2025, first of its kind in the US

w: Jean Nouvel reinvented the former Grands Magasins du Louvre as a mechanical organism: five 200-tonne floors rise and fall independently, reconfiguring the galleries into over 150,000 possible layouts. It reopened in October 2025 opposite the Louvre, trading a static museum for one that physically rearranges itself.
s: A museum with floors that rise and fall
why: Reopened Oct 2025 in a radically reconfigurable Jean Nouvel building

w: Zaha Hadid Architects' final major Chinese project reads as one sculpted volume that stretches westward into terraced parkland, its smooth concrete skin folding into outdoor terraces and skylit halls. Opened in 2025 beside Guangming Science Park, it anchors the district as a new civic and scientific landmark.
s: One sculpted concrete volume folding into a park
why: Opened 2025, one of ZHA's last completed major works

w: A permanent 10,000-square-metre digital-art complex opened October 2025 near Kyoto Station, darkened halls filled with over fifty projection works built around living, breathing phenomena rather than fixed images. Rooms respond to movement, spinning vortexes of light and colour through mirrored chambers.
s: Fifty rooms of breathing, responsive digital art
why: Opened October 2025 with never-before-seen teamLab works

w: Opened December 2025 beside the Louvre Abu Dhabi, this vast immersive hall lets suspended tree roots drape from the ceiling around clusters of stone rising from the floor, alongside glowing massless spheres drifting through darkened space. It is teamLab's most ambitious permanent installation outside Japan.
s: Suns and hanging roots suspended in darkness
why: New permanent teamLab flagship opened Dec 2025 in Saadiyat's culture district

w: Sixteen 3D-printed concrete columns, up to twelve feet tall, rise in a clearing in a former Soviet military zone deep in Bohemian forest, part of an effort to revive one of seventeen villages abandoned after the Cold War. Atelier Partero set raw high-performance concrete inside a genuinely wild, overgrown clearing.
s: 3D-printed concrete totems in a Cold War forest
why: Completed 2024, first phase of reviving a Cold War ghost valley

w: One of Richard Serra's late outdoor works stands on a 12,000-acre working ranch below the Beartooth Mountains: colossal steel plates leaning into each other across open range, rusted to the colour of the surrounding grasses. Reachable only by guided tour, it turns raw industrial sculpture into a Montana pilgrimage.
s: Serra's rusted steel plates on a Montana ranch
why: A Richard Serra land-art piece at a remote working-ranch sculpture park

w: Zaha Hadid Architects' curling 390-metre footbridge weaves around three arches where China's Grand Canal meets the Qiantang River, its steel ribbons echoing Hangzhou's silk-embroidery heritage. Completed in 2025, it is the centrepiece of a new riverside park stitching the historic canal to the modern city.
s: A silk-ribbon footbridge over the canal's mouth
why: Completed 2025, ZHA's centrepiece for a new Grand Canal park

w: Rising on a single 443-foot cable-stayed pylon, this is likely the world's longest pedestrian-and-tram bridge, stretching nearly three-quarters of a mile to link the new Kruunuvuori district to central Helsinki. Engineered to last two centuries, it is among the largest infrastructure builds in the city's history.
s: A 443ft pylon bridge built to last 200 years
why: Opened 2025 as one of the world's longest pedestrian/tram bridges

w: gmp Architects and bbp: architekten spent six years rebuilding the postwar concert hall inside Kiel Castle, renewing its acoustics while preserving the 1960s modernist shell overlooking the Kiel Fjord. Completed in 2025, it gives the Kiel Philharmonic a technically modern home inside a mid-century landmark.
s: A 1960s modernist hall reborn on the Kiel Fjord
why: Reopened 2025 after a six-year renewal, new Kiel Philharmonic home

n: Józef Świder State Music School Concert Hall
w: A corrugated, mirror-bright steel skin wraps this cube-shaped extension to a traditional Silesian music school, by local studio SLAS Architekci. Completed in 2025, its 362-seat hall gives young musicians a professional stage while the reflective facade dissolves the building into the sky and rooftops around it.
s: A mirror-steel cube for a Silesian music school
why: New 2025 concert hall wrapped in mirrored corrugated steel

w: Diller Scofidio + Renfro designed the Muslim world's first purpose-built mosque for women, its stone roof swelling upward to crown a prayer hall lit by skylights before sloping down over classrooms and social spaces. Completed 2025, it was conceived by Sheikha Moza bint Nasser for women's worship and scholarship.
s: First purpose-built mosque built for women
why: Completed 2025, a landmark first for contemporary Islamic architecture

w: Five twisted cuboid volumes, one per Pillar of Islam, stack and rotate around the prayer hall until they form an eight-pointed star seen from above. Kuwait-based Babnimnim Design Studio completed this neighbourhood mosque with lancet-cut facades borrowed from Mamluk-era Cairo, reworked in raw contemporary concrete.
s: Five twisted volumes forming a star from above
why: A 2023 reinterpretation of Mamluk architecture drawing global design press

w: Handcrafted zellige tilework and mashrabiya screens wrap 2,500 square metres of hydrothermal pools and a traditional hammam across two floors, crowned by a top-floor grooming suite with panoramic views over the White City. Opened as part of the hotel's 2024 rebirth, it won World's Best New Hotel Spa 2025.
s: Zellige-clad hammam crowning a reborn Art Deco hotel
why: Named World's Best New Hotel Spa 2025

w: Local stone and organic curves fold into the cliffs above Vroskopos Bay on the closest Cycladic island to Athens, in a spa resort blending indoor and outdoor treatment spaces with uninterrupted Aegean views. Recently opened, it won World's Best New Resort Spa 2025 for its minimalist reading of the island landscape.
s: Cliffside spa on the closest Cycladic isle
why: Named World's Best New Resort Spa 2025

w: Floating treatment pods and coral-mimicking pavilions rise from a private lagoon in the Maldives' Raa Atoll, built from sustainable materials as a wellness-first resort rather than a conventional beach hotel. It was named World's Best Spa Design 2025 for architecture that treats the reef itself as the design brief.
s: A resort built to mimic a living coral reef
why: Named World's Best Spa Design 2025

w: Central Asia's first major private museum of modern art opened September 2025 across two intersecting wings, one clad in rugged Jura limestone, the other in sleek aluminium, echoing the jagged Zailiyskiy Alatau mountains ringing the city. Founded by entrepreneur Nurlan Smagulov, it spans over 10,000 square metres.
s: Limestone and aluminium wings echoing the Alatau peaks
why: Opened Sept 2025, Central Asia's first private contemporary art museum

w: Tadao Ando's tenth building for the Benesse Art Site sinks two storeys into a hillside above the Seto Inland Sea, its charred-black walls and sweeping sloped roof following the land's contours rather than fighting them. Opened in May 2025, it deepens Naoshima's shift from quiet fishing island to global art pilgrimage.
s: Ando's tenth Naoshima building, sunk into a hillside
why: Opened May 2025, Tadao Ando's newest work on Japan's art island

area: Here East, Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park
w: Diller Scofidio + Renfro converted a 2012 Olympics media hangar into an open-storage museum where 250,000 objects, 350,000 books and 1,000 archives sit visible on towering shelving, from a Frank Lloyd Wright office to Glastonbury stage fragments. Opened May 2025, it turns the V&A's working archive into the exhibition.
s: 250,000 museum objects on open, walkable shelving
why: Opened May 2025, an entire working archive turned into a public museum

w: Named after the Dharug word for storyteller, this curved oval library breaks from the rigid street grid of Western Sydney, its rounded form and green roof inspired by the nearby Georges River. Opened as anchor of Liverpool's new Civic Place, it holds two kilometres of shelving behind a round-windowed facade.
s: An oval, round-windowed 'storyteller' library
why: New civic anchor for Western Sydney's fastest-growing city centre

w: An abandoned, never-finished Brutalist shell in the Labone district was reclaimed November 2025 as an experimental art and research space, its bare structural bones left exposed rather than clad. Curators treat the building's incompleteness as the point, staging residencies inside raw, unplastered concrete frames.
s: An unfinished concrete shell turned exhibition space
why: Opened Nov 2025 inside a deliberately unfinished Brutalist frame

n: Anthony Timberlands Center for Design and Materials Innovation
w: Grafton Architects' first US building centres an 11,000-square-foot double-height timber workshop, with a lecture hall suspended directly above so students watch fabrication in progress through the floor. Dedicated August 2025, the mass-timber structure doubles as a research lab for Arkansas's wood-products industry.
s: A lecture hall suspended over a working timber shop
why: Grafton Architects' first US project, dedicated Aug 2025

w: Cadence Architects raised this monumental exposed-concrete library on pilotis at the heart of an engineering campus, completed March 2025, deliberately positioned as a crossroads linking hostels to academic blocks rather than a quiet, isolated reading hall. Its raw board-formed concrete gives the campus a new anchor.
s: A raised concrete library anchoring a tech campus
why: Completed March 2025, a bold concrete landmark for Bangalore's tech campuses
